analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing consumers into binding arbitration in standard-form contracts.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2002 with no cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Many companies write a clause into their standard contracts — for credit cards, phones, rentals, loans — requiring that any dispute go to a private arbitrator chosen under industry rules, with no judge, no jury, and no appeal. This bill would make such forced-arbitration clauses an unfair and deceptive trade practice and unenforceable. Consumers could still agree to arbitration after a dispute actually arises, when the choice is genuine. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Any individual who signs a standard consumer contract — credit card holders, borrowers, renters, phone and utility customers. When a company wrongs them, they could take the dispute to court or join a class action instead of being pushed into a private arbitration process the company helped set up.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with credit cards, loans, and contracts

how_it_helps.text: Makes any written provision in a consumer transaction or contract requiring binding arbitration an unfair and deceptive trade practice that is not enforceable [S2][S3].

Covers a wide range of consumer dealings — sales and rentals of goods, services, and real property, plus credit and other financial products — and applies to any individual, not just defined consumer categories [S3].
Still allows arbitration where both parties agree in writing after a dispute has actually arisen, so voluntary arbitration remains available [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, phone companies, and other businesses that use standard-form contracts, which would lose their ability to steer disputes into private arbitration and would face court suits, including class actions, instead.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, phone companies, and contract-based businesses

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that arbitration is often faster and cheaper for an individual consumer than a court case, and that class actions can take years and deliver most of their value to attorneys; the bill's supporters respond that forced arbitration is agreed to before any dispute exists, so the consumer's consent is not meaningful [S3].
The bill would override any federal or state arbitration law inconsistent with it, to the extent of the inconsistency, so it displaces existing legal arrangements governing arbitration [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is real: a guaranteed day in court when a company breaks a contract it wrote itself. The cost falls on businesses, which lose a system that typically resolves individual disputes cheaply for them and shields them from class-wide liability. The bill left the tradeoff unaddressed only in the sense that it never went anywhere: with no hearing and no cosponsors, its design was never tested or refined in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee and a subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on July 18, 2002 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 1, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No member signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor count was zero [S4].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that write forced-arbitration clauses into their contracts — banks, credit card issuers, telecom and utility companies — kept a dispute system they control, and their customers kept losing their access to court. Consumers gained nothing from this bill's death.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: Their standard loan and card contracts typically require cardholders and borrowers to take disputes to private arbitration; the bill would make those clauses unenforceable and expose them to court suits and class actions [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Telecom, utility, and other subscription businesses
industries.note: Cell phone, internet, and service agreements routinely impose forced arbitration; the bill would cover these contracts and let customers sue in court instead [S3].
The commercial arbitration industry's volume of consumer cases comes largely from clauses the bill would ban, so its fee revenue would shrink substantially [S2][S3].
